domain.name: Backend Engineer
domain.description: From HTTP and databases to production-grade APIs and distributed systems.

skills.name: Programming Fundamentals
skills.description: Core language concepts: variables, control flow, functions, and data types.

skills.name: HTTP and REST
skills.description: Understand HTTP verbs, status codes, headers, and RESTful API design.

skills.name: Git and Version Control
skills.description: Track changes, branch, merge, and collaborate with Git and GitHub.

skills.name: SQL and Relational Databases
skills.description: Model data, write queries, and design normalized schemas.

skills.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
skills.description: Choose the right data structure and analyze algorithmic complexity.

skills.name: Web Frameworks
skills.description: Build HTTP servers with a modern framework (Express, FastAPI, Django, etc.).

skills.name: API Design
skills.description: Design clean, versioned, well-documented APIs that clients love.

skills.name: Error Handling and Logging
skills.description: Structure errors, propagate them cleanly, and log useful context.

skills.name: Testing
skills.description: Write unit, integration, and end-to-end tests that catch real bugs.

skills.name: Authentication and Authorization
skills.description: Implement sessions, JWTs, OAuth, and role-based access control.

skills.name: Caching
skills.description: Speed up reads with in-memory, Redis, and HTTP caching strategies.

skills.name: Message Queues
skills.description: Decouple services with queues and workers (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS).

skills.name: ORM and Migrations
skills.description: Use an ORM safely and evolve schemas with backward-compatible migrations.

skills.name: Docker and Containers
skills.description: Package apps into portable images and run them consistently.

skills.name: CI/CD Pipelines
skills.description: Automate tests, builds, and deploys with GitHub Actions or similar.

skills.name: Database Performance
skills.description: Read query plans, add indexes, and avoid N+1 queries.

skills.name: Monitoring and Observability
skills.description: Track metrics, logs, and traces to know how your service behaves.

skills.name: Distributed Systems
skills.description: Reason about consistency, partitioning, and failure modes at scale.

skills.name: Security Best Practices
skills.description: Prevent OWASP top 10 issues, handle secrets, and secure inputs.

skills.name: System Design
skills.description: Design scalable services considering tradeoffs, failure, and cost.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is idempotent and typically used to fully replace a resource?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces a resource idempotently — repeating the call yields the same final state.

questions.prompt: What does HTTP 404 mean?
questions.explanation: 404 = resource not found. 401 = unauthenticated, 403 = forbidden, 500 = server error.

questions.prompt: Which git command creates a new local branch and switches to it?
questions.explanation: Both `git switch -c` (modern) and `git checkout -b` (classic) create and switch in one step.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of feature branches in Git?

options.text: Isolate work so main stays stable

questions.explanation: Feature branches keep experimental work off main until it's reviewed and ready.

questions.prompt: Which SQL constraint ensures a column uniquely identifies each row?
questions.explanation: A PRIMARY KEY is unique and not null — one per table, uniquely identifying rows.

questions.prompt: What does database normalization primarily reduce?
questions.explanation: Normalization removes duplicate data so updates, inserts, and deletes stay consistent.

questions.prompt: Average time complexity of looking up a key in a hash table?
questions.explanation: With a good hash function and low load factor, lookups are amortized O(1).

questions.prompt: Which data structure is best for a LIFO order of operations?
questions.explanation: A stack follows LIFO — push and pop from the same end.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT typically a core part of a web framework like Express or FastAPI?
questions.explanation: Web frameworks handle HTTP concerns; the database engine is separate (Postgres, MySQL, etc.).

questions.prompt: What is middleware in a web server?

options.text: Code that runs between the request and the handler (auth, logging, etc.)

questions.explanation: Middleware intercepts requests to run cross-cutting concerns — auth, logging, rate limiting — before/after handlers.

questions.prompt: Which is the best sign of a well-designed REST API?

options.text: Resources are nouns; verbs come from HTTP methods

questions.explanation: REST resources are nouns (/users/42) and actions come from HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE).

questions.prompt: Why version APIs (e.g., /v1/users)?

options.text: To ship breaking changes without breaking existing clients

questions.explanation: Versioning lets you evolve the API while old clients keep working against older versions.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of structured logging?

options.text: Make logs searchable and machine-parseable (JSON, key-value)

questions.explanation: Structured logs (e.g., JSON) can be filtered, aggregated, and alerted on by log platforms.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status is best for an unexpected server error?
questions.explanation: 500 = Internal Server Error. 4xx is for client errors, 5xx for server errors.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a unit test and an integration test?

options.text: Unit tests isolate a single unit; integration tests exercise multiple parts together

questions.explanation: Unit tests verify one function in isolation; integration tests verify components work together (e.g., service + DB).

questions.prompt: What is a test double (mock/stub)?

options.text: A fake object that stands in for a real dependency during a test

questions.explanation: Test doubles let you control the behavior of external dependencies (APIs, DBs) for fast, isolated tests.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: AuthN verifies identity; AuthZ decides what they can do

questions.explanation: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?'

questions.prompt: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is best described as:

options.text: A signed token containing claims, verifiable without a DB lookup

questions.explanation: JWTs are signed (not necessarily encrypted) so the server can verify authenticity from the token itself.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of caching?

options.text: Reduce latency and load on slower downstream services

questions.explanation: Caching trades a small staleness risk for much lower latency and reduced backend pressure.

questions.prompt: Which is the classic cache invalidation risk?

options.text: Serving stale data after the source has changed

questions.explanation: Without a good invalidation strategy (TTL, event-driven), cached values can become inconsistent with the source.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of message queues?

options.text: Decouple producers and consumers so slow work can run asynchronously

questions.explanation: Queues let producers push events and consumers process at their own pace, absorbing bursts and isolating failures.

questions.prompt: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) is used to:

options.text: Map objects in code to database tables and rows

questions.explanation: ORMs like Prisma, SQLAlchemy, or ActiveRecord let you work with typed objects instead of raw SQL.

questions.prompt: What is the key principle of safe database migrations?

options.text: Combine all schema changes into one big migration
Make changes backward-compatible so old and new code can coexist during rollout

questions.explanation: Zero-downtime migrations avoid breaking changes: add columns as nullable, backfill, then switch reads/writes, then drop later.

questions.prompt: What is a Docker image?

options.text: A read-only template used to create containers

questions.explanation: Images are immutable blueprints; containers are the running instances.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of containers over virtual machines?

options.text: Share the host kernel — smaller, faster to start

questions.explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel, making them lightweight and fast compared to full VMs.

questions.prompt: Continuous Integration (CI) primarily means:

options.text: Deploy to production on every commit
Automatically build and test every change

questions.explanation: CI runs automated builds and tests on every push, catching regressions early.

questions.prompt: What is a blue/green deployment?

options.text: Run two identical environments and switch traffic between them for zero-downtime releases

questions.explanation: Blue/green runs old (blue) and new (green) side by side, then flips the router — easy rollback if issues arise.

questions.prompt: What is an N+1 query problem?

options.text: One query for a list + one query per item, causing N+1 total round trips

questions.explanation: Fetching a list then querying per item explodes into N+1 queries. Fix: JOIN, batch, or use dataloader-style batching.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a database index?

options.text: Speed up reads at the cost of slower writes and extra storage

questions.explanation: Indexes are lookup structures (usually B-trees) that trade write cost for much faster reads.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the three pillars of observability?
questions.explanation: Metrics, logs, and traces are the three pillars. Backups are important but not part of observability.

questions.prompt: What is a p99 latency metric?

options.text: The latency below which 99% of requests complete

questions.explanation: p99 captures tail latency — often more important than the average for user experience.

questions.prompt: The CAP theorem says a distributed system can only guarantee two of:
questions.explanation: Under a network partition, you choose consistency (reject writes) or availability (serve stale data).

questions.prompt: Eventual consistency means:

options.text: All replicas will converge to the same value given enough time without new writes

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency trades immediate consistency for availability and scale — used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, etc.

questions.prompt: Which is the OWASP-recommended defense against SQL injection?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL structure from data — user input can never become executable SQL.

questions.prompt: The principle of least privilege means:

options.text: Grant only the permissions needed for a task — nothing more

questions.explanation: Minimal permissions limit blast radius if credentials leak or a service is compromised.

questions.prompt: Horizontal scaling means:

options.text: Adding more machines behind a load balancer

questions.explanation: Horizontal = scale out (many machines); vertical = scale up (one bigger machine).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a load balancer?

options.text: Distribute traffic across multiple backend instances and health-check them

questions.explanation: Load balancers spread requests, remove unhealthy nodes, and often terminate TLS.

questions.prompt: What does 'stateless' mean for a service?

options.text: Requests carry all needed context so any instance can handle any request

questions.explanation: Stateless services scale horizontally without sticky sessions — session state lives in a DB/cache, not in-process memory.

questions.prompt: Which is the best reason to choose a message queue over a synchronous call between services?

options.text: Resilience to consumer downtime and traffic spikes

questions.explanation: Queues buffer work and let slow or down consumers catch up without breaking producers.

questions.prompt: Which is the primary purpose of a function in programming?

options.text: Encapsulate reusable logic with a name and inputs

questions.explanation: Functions group reusable logic, take inputs, and return outputs — a core abstraction in every language.

questions.prompt: What is a variable in programming?

options.text: A named reference to a value in memory

questions.explanation: Variables bind names to values so you can reference and update data in your program.

questions.prompt: Which pattern handles repeated consumer failures in a message queue?

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff and a dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: Backoff prevents thundering-herd retries; the dead-letter queue isolates poison messages for human inspection.
